name: Cellon Oak

location.address: Cellon Oak Park, 4100 NW 169th Place, Gainesville, FL 32653 (near LaCrosse, Alachua County)

official_register.name: Florida Forest Service Champion Trees register (PK 199, Florida Co-Champion Live Oak)

access: Free. Alachua County park bought by the county in 1989 (WUFT 2019); a mown 10-acre lawn around a single tree, two picnic tables and a grill, no restrooms. Third-party app lists 8 AM to 7 PM daily (not the county's own page; confirm). Closed 10 to 11 April 2025 for a lightning-protection installation, reopened after (WCJB).
transport: About 19 km north-west of central Gainesville and the University of Florida; no public transport verified. By car only as far as this pass found.

A 2019/2023 WUFT piece says it is the Florida co-champion; WUFT 2023: the title passed in October 2022 to a bigger-trunked live oak on private land in Alachua (36.5 ft around, 78 ft tall, crown 180 ft); Cellon Oak is about 13 ft taller. Species size check: 991 cm is 118% of the species reference of 843 cm (n=11, species_size.py). Nobody cored it. Held broad. CONDITION per blog (not a source for facts): lightning rods, cable support for a large limb. story:
Alachua County bought ten acres in 1989 for the sake of one tree, and the park is still just that. A mown lawn, two picnic tables, a grill and the Cellon Oak.

The Florida Forest Service's champion tree register measured it in 2018 at 390 inches around, about 9.9 metres, 91 feet tall, with a crown spreading 171 feet. The register lists it as Florida's co-champion live oak. In October 2022, WUFT reported, the title passed to a live oak on private land elsewhere in Alachua with a thicker trunk, 36.5 feet round. The Cellon Oak is still about 13 feet the taller of the two.

Its age is an estimate. A 2019 WUFT caption put its planting at about 1832, a local television station says more than 200 years, and nobody has cored it. A blog's 300 to 500 years has nothing behind it.

Lightning is what worries the county. In April 2025 it closed the park for two days to fit a new lightning protection system, meant to keep a strike from killing the tree.

You will see the name spelled Ceylon in some older reports. Cellon is the park's own spelling. The park lies near LaCrosse, about 19 km north-west of central Gainesville and the University of Florida. We found no public transport, so plan on a car. Entry is free, a third-party listing gives the hours as 8 in the morning to 7 at night, and there are no restrooms.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the single tree the park's mown ten-acre lawn is kept around, 91 feet tall with a crown spreading 171 feet. It stands in Cellon Oak Park, near LaCrosse north-west of Gainesville.
